name: IoT telemetry platform
description: Device fleets speak MQTT to an edge broker, a managed ingestion service absorbs the firehose into the cloud, a time-series database stores and serves recent telemetry with retention policies, and a stream processor downsamples raw readings into the rollups that long-term analytics actually query. The pattern's defining constraints come from the edge: flaky connectivity (devices buffer and burst), clock skew (event time is unreliable), fleet-wide schema drift across firmware versions, and cardinality explosions when per-device series multiply by sensor count. Downsampling is not an optimization but the survival mechanism — raw millisecond readings are unaffordable to keep hot forever.
when_to_use: Choose this when you operate a real device fleet — sensors, vehicles, machines, meters — producing continuous telemetry that must drive monitoring, alerting, and historical analysis.
It fits when per-device series counts and ingest rates rule out a general-purpose database, and when retention economics demand tiered raw-to-rollup storage.
Fleet scale makes per-device polling impossible; telemetry must stream in.
when_not_to_use: Skip the MQTT edge if your 'devices' are actually servers or apps — that is log/clickstream collection (10) over HTTP.
A few hundred devices at low frequency fit happily in Postgres/Timescale without Kinesis or Flink in between.
And if telemetry only feeds daily reports, batch-land it in the lake and skip the time-series serving layer entirely.

hot_spots.title: Edge connectivity
hot_spots.detail: Flaky device links create late, duplicated, or out-of-order readings.

hot_spots.title: Series cardinality
hot_spots.detail: Millions of unique series explode index memory in the time-series store.

hot_spots.title: Downsampling policy
hot_spots.detail: Aggressive rollups quietly destroy the raw detail investigations need.

hot_spots.title: Clock skew
hot_spots.detail: Drifting device clocks corrupt time-window aggregations.

stages.name: Edge
stages.role: MQTT broker terminating device connections — the corpus has no dedicated MQTT broker (Mosquitto/EMQX/HiveMQ), so the closest picks are general brokers with MQTT support
stages.rationale: The honest recommendation is a dedicated MQTT broker (EMQX, HiveMQ, or cloud IoT Core services) — none are in the corpus, so RabbitMQ stands in as the nearest real entry: its MQTT plugin handles moderate fleets and many teams already run it. NATS is lightweight with an MQTT interface and shines in constrained environments; Azure Event Hubs and its IoT sibling provide the managed MQTT front door on Azure. Whatever terminates MQTT, keep it thin: authenticate devices, absorb QoS/reconnect semantics, and hand off to the cloud stream immediately.

stages.name: Ingest
stages.role: Managed cloud stream absorbing the aggregated device firehose for fan-out
stages.rationale: Kinesis is the doc's pick for good reason in AWS-centric IoT: fully managed, IoT Core integrates natively, and shard-based scaling matches bursty fleet traffic without broker operations. Kafka (or Redpanda) wins when you need longer retention for replay, richer ecosystem fan-out, or are avoiding cloud lock-in — at the cost of running it. Event Hubs is the Azure equivalent with MQTT-adjacent integration; Pub/Sub on GCP. The choice mostly follows the cloud your fleet management already lives in.

stages.name: Raw archive
stages.role: Cheap immutable archive of raw telemetry for replay and ML training
stages.rationale: Cheap immutable object storage as the landing layer decouples ingestion from processing: replays, backfills, and audits read the raw dump instead of re-extracting from sources.

stages.name: Time-series store
stages.role: Store telemetry with time-partitioning, compression, and retention policies; serve device and fleet queries
stages.rationale: TimescaleDB is Postgres underneath — hypertables, columnar compression, continuous aggregates, and retention policies, plus full SQL and joins against device metadata tables, which pure time-series stores make painful. That relational interoperability is usually decisive for IoT, where telemetry means nothing without the device registry. InfluxDB fits metrics-native workflows and edge deployments; QuestDB wins on raw ingest speed per node; ClickHouse when telemetry analytics grows into general OLAP; VictoriaMetrics for Prometheus-shaped infrastructure-style monitoring of the fleet.

stages.name: Downsample
stages.role: Continuously aggregate raw readings into 1m/1h rollups; enforce tiered retention
stages.rationale: Flink's event-time windows with watermarks handle exactly what device data throws at you — late, out-of-order readings from buffering devices — producing correct rollups where wall-clock aggregation quietly lies. That said, check the store first: Timescale's continuous aggregates cover simple rollups without any streaming engine, and only reach for Flink when downsampling needs cross-stream enrichment or complex logic. Spark Structured Streaming fits Spark shops; Kafka Streams for JVM-embedded simplicity; Bytewax when the team is Python-first.
